newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. retreats from remarks on Canadian salmon row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. retreats from remarks on Canadian salmon row.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley on Tuesday backtracked from comments which suggested that an illegal blockade of an Alaskan ferry by Canadian fishermen had forced the two sides to focus on solving their salmon dispute.
And the Canadian government quickly moved to try to quell encouragement of any vigilante action in the future.
"What I was trying to express was an opinion that obviously there was a lot of attention as a result of those illegal activities," Daley said at a hastily arranged meeting with reporters.
"But those sort of actions are going to do nothing in the short term and long term but cause further separation and inability to bring this matter to resolution."

Canadian fishermen blockaded the ferry in the British Columbia port of Prince Rupert for three days last month to protest against what they claimed was overfishing of salmon by their U.S. counterparts in Alaska.

The fracas prompted visits to Washington by Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy and Fisheries Minister David Anderson, and subsequent to the blockade the two countries appointed top representatives to try to reach a solution.

Daley had told reporters in Montreal on Monday: "Obviously the actions that occurred a couple of weeks ago, and the fact that negotiations just weren't going anywhere, forced the governments to look at it differently."
He also said: "Maybe we have gotten to the point, based upon the activities ... where everyone understands that there must be a solution to this problem."

Canadian Trade Minister Sergio Marchi, standing at Daley's side, said the process to choose the new representatives -- Canada's David Strangway and the United States' William Ruckelshaus -- had been under way before the blockade.
"We don't believe either on the Canadian side that illegal activities brings either side closer to a resolution," Marchi said.

Foreign Minister Axworthy suggested in a separate news conference with Anderson and Strangway that the blockade may actually have helped turn the U.S. government against the Canadian request to submit the salmon issue to arbitration.
"The chance of getting that (binding arbitration) was not helped by the kind of confrontation that was taking place," he said.
The two countries demonstrated on Tuesday that they have given up any serious hope of reaching an agreement on limiting and sharing out the salmon catch this season.
Daley said everyone would like to see an agreement this season but it "probably will take a little longer than trying to expect some resolution in the next number of weeks before the season is over."

Strangway said he hoped to begin meeting with Ruckelshaus in the next few days but would only be making his report by the end of the year, with the aim of having an agreement by the start of fishing next summer.

Both sides also took aim directly or indirectly at maverick British Columbia Premier Glen Clark, who has threatened to shut down a torpedo testing range at Nanoose Bay used by both Canada and the U.S.
Canadian Defence Minister Art Eggleton called on Clark to separate Nanoose from salmon while Daley said, without naming Clark, that "inflammatory comments ... only spread people apart."
